question.prompt: Let \(1,\) \(4,\) \(\ldots\) and \(9,\) \(16,\) \(\ldots\) be two arithmetic progressions. The set \(S\) is the union of the first \(2004\) terms of each sequence. How many distinct numbers are in \(S?\)

solutions.explanation:
Each progression has \(2004\) distinct terms because its common difference is positive. Adding their sizes gives \(4008\), but every number appearing in both progressions has then been counted twice.

The common differences are \(3\) and \(7\). The last included terms are
\[
\begin{aligned}
1+3(2004-1)&=6010,\\
9+7(2004-1)&=14030.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus a common included term must lie between \(9\) and \(6010\).

The second progression begins \(9,16,\ldots\). Since \(9\) is absent from the first progression and \(16\) belongs to both, \(16\) is the first common term. The difference between any two common terms must be divisible by both \(3\) and \(7\), hence by their least common multiple, \(21\). Conversely, adding \(21\) moves seven steps along the first progression and three steps along the second. Therefore all common terms are exactly
\[
16,\ 16+21,\ 16+2(21),\ldots
\]
up to the shared upper bound.

Now
\[
16+285(21)=6001\leq6010,
\]
while the next term is \(6022>6010\). There are therefore \(286\) common terms, including the first one. Subtracting each duplicated number once gives
\[
|S|=2004+2004-286=3722.
\]
The answer is \(3722\), choice A.
solutions.title: Count the overlap using common steps
